description:
What we focus on

We work on problems where science, engineering and software meet: space medicine and astronaut health, mission operations, Earth and planetary data, and autonomous systems for missions where real-time support from Earth is not possible. Our approach is evidence-driven. We start from published NASA data and research, build mathematical and computational models, and turn them into usable prototypes rather than concepts on slides.
summary:
Astronaut Health Monitor (AHM) 

Astronaut Health Monitor is an offline-first, installable web app that lets each crew member on a long space mission check their own health every day, without relying on a connection to Earth.

Astronauts complete a short guided check-in: symptoms, manually entered measurements (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, temperature, sleep, exercise, hydration) and mood. A deterministic, explainable rule engine then turns this into a clear green/yellow/red/critical status, showing exactly which rule and value triggered it, with plain-language actions and escalation steps. An interactive 3D body, trend charts, reminders, learning pages on spaceflight health risks, and gentle gamification keep crews engaged. Commanders and flight surgeons get a read-only crew overview, and data syncs to ground when a link is available.

This matters because communication delays on Moon and Mars missions make real-time medical support from Earth impossible. Crews need to spot problems early and act autonomously, and AHM gives them a transparent, private tool that works with zero internet.

details:
Astronaut Health Monitor (AHM): Project Details

What it does and how it works

AHM is that lets every crew member run a daily health self-assessment with no internet connection.

1. Register and unlock. Each astronaut registers with a name, unique crew ID, role, environment and mission dates, then unlocks their profile with a PIN. A fresh install has no astronauts and no data.

2. Daily check-in. A guided wizard covers a recap of yesterday's advice, symptoms with severity, manually entered measurements (heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, SpO2, sleep, exercise, hydration, weight, optional radiation), and mood and stress, including a safety question.

3. Rule engine. A deterministic engine checks each value against threshold bands, combination rules (for example hypoxia or decompression sickness patterns) and multi-day trend rules. It returns a green, yellow, red or critical status, and the worst status wins.

4. Explainable result. Every status shows the rule ID and the value that triggered it, plus plain-language actions. Red and critical results always show an escalation block.

5. Visual tools. The app includes a home dashboard, trend charts with threshold bands and a personal baseline, and an interactive 3D anatomical body where each organ glows with its current status and opens a panel explaining its function, spaceflight effects and the astronaut's latest values.

6. Support features. There are reminders and notifications that fire offline, Learn pages on spaceflight health risks with sources, environment-specific tips (spacecraft, station, rover, Moon base, Mars base), and points, streaks and badges.

7. Crew oversight and sync. Commanders and flight surgeons get a read-only crew overview with surgeon notes and an audit log. When a link is available, data syncs to a ground server in the background and keeps both versions if there is a conflict.

Benefits

- Works without Earth. All reads and writes go to the device first, and the network is never required.

- Transparent. There is no black box; every result can be traced to a specific rule and value.

- Private. Astronauts see only their own data, protected by a PIN.

- Early detection. Trend and combination rules can catch patterns that a single reading would miss.

- Low hardware needs. It runs in a browser on any tablet or laptop, with no sensors or wearables.

Intended impact

On Moon and Mars missions, communication delays of up to about 20 minutes each way and blackout periods make real-time medical support impossible. AHM is meant to support crew medical autonomy by helping astronauts notice problems early, know what to do next and know when to escalate. The same design could serve other isolated settings such as Antarctic stations, submarines, remote clinics and disaster zones.

No special hardware is needed: any device with a modern browser will run it.

How it is creative

- 3D body as the interface. Health status is shown on real anatomical geometry that the astronaut can rotate and tap, instead of in a table of numbers.

- One rule set, two engines. The rule engine exists in both TypeScript (on the device) and Python (on the server), and both are tested against the same shared test vectors, so ground and crew get the same answer.

- Gamification with guardrails. There are no points for reporting symptoms, no shaming on red days and no rewards for unsafe behaviour.

- Environment awareness. Tips and rule modifiers change with the habitat type and mission phase. For example, the first seven days soften only yellow results, never red or critical.

Factors we considered

- Connectivity: we treated zero internet as the normal case, not the exception.

- Honesty of data: input is manual only, with no simulated, seeded or generated health data anywhere in the app.

- Medical safety: the rules are deterministic with no AI at runtime, the app names no drugs or doses, a disclaimer appears at onboarding and on results, and thresholds are defaults to be verified by medical professionals.

- Accessibility: colour is never the only signal (it is paired with an icon and text), touch targets are at least 44px, reduced-motion is respected, and the 3D body has a keyboard-accessible alternative and a 2D fallback.

- Privacy and roles: every record is scoped per astronaut, oversight roles are read-only, and views are audited.

- Data integrity: sync is idempotent and never loses data on conflict.

- Licensing and attribution: NASA risk information is paraphrased with sources, third-party assets are credited, and the app loads no external CDNs, fonts or analytics.

- Limitations: this is a self-assessment aid, not a diagnostic device, and it is not endorsed by NASA.
